process_teaching.prerequisite_note: Use the terminal and owner information from file foundations/access policy. This lesson introduces processes, IDs and pausing.

concepts.title: A process is one program instance
concepts.text: A running program has a process ID, or PID. Several instances can share the same name, so check the owner as well as the name. This terminal acts as the user shown above it; every displayed process is simulated.

concepts.title: Read a snapshot before acting
concepts.text: ps shows a snapshot. PID identifies a process, PPID identifies its parent, USER is its owner, NI is its nice value (a priority preference taught later) and COMMAND is its executable name. Read the first STAT letter: R is running, S is waiting and T is paused. Other letters give extra details.

concepts.title: Find a name without ignoring its owner
concepts.text: pgrep -u morgan -x archiver lists PIDs matching Morgan and the full archiver name. A name alone can still match several instances. This subset accepts ordinary names without special pattern characters; inspect the returned PID with ps before acting.

concepts.title: kill sends a request; it does not always end a program
concepts.text: Despite its name, kill sends a signal. STOP pauses a process while keeping it present; CONT continues it. A successful request often prints nothing, so inspect ps afterward. The example pauses Morgan’s archiver with different PIDs from the assignment. TERM can leave an ending request waiting while a program is paused, so do not send it when the goal is a pause.

process_teaching.inputs: Morgan’s archiver is running in a separate virtual process table. Your assignment table is untouched.
process_teaching.try_change: After pausing the archiver, type kill -CONT 6010 and run it, then inspect its state again. It should be present with R as its first state letter.

process_teaching.prerequisite_note: First practice pausing a process and reading its state. This lesson explains why an ending request can wait while a process is paused.

concepts.title: Paused work cannot act on an ordinary ending request yet
concepts.text: TERM asks a program to end; in this exercise workers use its normal ending behavior. When a worker is paused, that request remains pending until it can run again. Sending TERM repeatedly does not itself continue the worker.

concepts.title: Continue a pending request, or end immediately
concepts.text: CONT lets a paused worker run again, including receiving a pending TERM. KILL ends the modeled worker even while paused. Real applications may handle or ignore TERM; KILL cannot be handled. This fixed model excludes uninterruptible waits and custom handlers.

concepts.title: An absent result is useful verification
concepts.text: After the worker ends it disappears from ps and pgrep. A query selecting only its old PID can return no rows and status 1. That is an expected no-match result, not unsupported syntax. The simulator explicitly labels nonzero status rather than pretending the command printed that note.

process_teaching.inputs: Morgan’s packer begins running in its own practice table. The example first pauses it and queues TERM before continuing it.

This exercise models scheduling preferences, not actual performance or CPU percentages.

process_teaching.prerequisite_note: Use ps and process ownership from the previous tasks. This lesson introduces the nice value and changing an existing process’s priority preference.

concepts.title: A larger nice value means lower urgency
concepts.text: A nice value is a scheduling preference. Raising it makes a process more willing to yield CPU time; it does not pause or end the process. A new program inherits its parent’s value: an ordinary unmodified shell commonly has nice 0. This activity supplies the starting values instead of launching programs.

concepts.title: Set an absolute value on the intended process
concepts.text: Use renice --priority with the requested absolute value and -p with the intended PID. The example sets nice to 5; it does not add 5. Read NI before and after. Choose the intended owner and executable, rather than every program with a similar name. N can appear after the first STAT letter when nice is positive.

concepts.title: Keep the permission boundary clear
concepts.text: Here alex or Morgan can raise their own process’s nice value but cannot lower it again under the fixed ordinary-user limits. Reset this example or attempt if you overshoot. Real resource limits/capabilities may differ. The model verifies values and continued presence; it does not measure real CPU speed.

process_teaching.inputs: Morgan’s catalogue process starts at nice 0 in a separate table. A different preview process should stay unchanged.
process_teaching.try_change: Reset this example only and use an absolute value 12 instead of 5. Inspect NI and confirm the process remains present. Trying to lower it back afterward is denied under this exercise’s limits.

scenarios.title: Complete a safe process handover
scenarios.summary: Retire an abandoned family, restore paused work and lower indexing urgency without disturbing healthy programs.
scenarios.objective:
Investigate alex’s process table before making changes. End old-run and its worker, while preserving live-run and its worker. Continue alex’s paused proofreader without changing its nice value 0. Set alex’s indexer to absolute nice 15 and keep it active. Preserve blair’s family, the reporting service, init and every other process setting.

Use parent IDs to distinguish the workers. Ending a controller alone does not end its child; record the intended PIDs before changing the family. Verify the complete handover with the current table. Supported action order and signal alternatives are accepted.

process_teaching.prerequisite_note: Combine process selection, pause/continue, termination and niceness from this unit. This capstone adds reasoning about parents and children.

concepts.title: A parent and its child are separate processes
concepts.text: PPID points to the parent. Ending a parent does not automatically end its child. In this fixed model, a child whose parent ends is adopted by init and reports PPID 1; real systems may also have subreapers or a temporary zombie/wait stage, which are not modeled here.

concepts.title: Identify the whole family before changing it
concepts.text: Two workers can have the same name and owner but belong to different controllers. Record the PIDs belonging to the old controller before ending it, because the child’s displayed parent can change afterward. A name-only selection is not enough for this assignment.

concepts.title: Plan a complete handover
concepts.text: The example ends an old parent and worker while preserving a live family, using different values from the assignment. Then apply the unit’s other skills independently: restore paused work and set the requested nice value without disturbing unrelated processes. Check all outcomes, not only the first repair.

process_teaching.inputs: Morgan has old-job and live-job families in a separate practice table. Both have a worker; the parent relationship tells them apart.
